title: Federal Power Act Section 202(c): Orlando Utilities Commission (OUC) Order No. 202-26-26
date_evidence: On June 4, 2026, the Department of Energy (DOE) issued emergency DOE Order No. 202-26-26, pursuant to section 202(c) of the Federal Power Act, to the Orlando Utilities Commission (OUC).
key_claim: DOE ordered the Orlando Utilities Commission to keep coal-fired Stanton Unit 1 available to operate from 4 June to 1 September 2026, halting its planned cold shutdown.
frame_summary: The Department of Energy asserts that an electricity reliability emergency justifies directing OUC to keep Stanton Unit 1 available past its planned shutdown, extending the pattern of federal retirement deferrals to Florida.
verbatim_quote: The order directs OUC to ensure that Unit 1 at the Stanton Energy Center (Stanton) in Orlando, Florida remains available to operate. This order is in effect beginning on June 4, 2026 through September 1, 2026.

title: 2026 Summer Reliability Assessment Snapshot
date_evidence: NERC issued the 2026 Summer Reliability Assessment on May 19, with record resource additions bolstering power readiness for the summer season, despite ongoing elevated risks in some areas.
key_claim: Record resource additions have strengthened summer readiness; elevated-risk regions fell from six in 2025 to three regions and one locality in 2026, while load growth rose 11 GW since 2025.
frame_summary: NERC argues the resource-adequacy picture improved materially on record solar, battery and gas additions, while demand acceleration and large loads remain the live risks in a shrinking set of regions.
verbatim_quote: In 2025, six regions were at an elevated risk for supply shortfalls in abnormal summer conditions. In 2026, only three regions and one locality are at-risk.
verbatim_list: Load growth has increased by 11 GW since 2025. This builds on the 10 GW growth in 2025, which doubled the increase from 2023–2024.
NERC’s assessment finds that record resource additions have strengthened readiness for the summer season, even as elevated risks remain in some areas.

title: PJM Capacity Auction Procures 138,318 MW of Generation Resources as Work Continues To Address Growing Electricity Demand
date_evidence: (Valley Forge, PA – July 14, 2026) – PJM Interconnection today announced the results of its 2028/2029 Base Residual Auction
key_claim: PJM's 2028/2029 capacity auction cleared at the FERC-approved cap of $325/MW-day, 6,831 MW short of the reliability requirement, and PJM plans a special Backstop Procurement in September.
frame_summary: PJM argues electricity demand is growing faster than supply, that back-to-back RTO-wide shortfalls justify a backstop procurement and connect-and-manage rules for large loads, and that the price collar protects consumers while reforms land.
verbatim_quote: The capacity of the resources procured in the auction, plus FRR resources, is short of PJM’s reliability requirement by 6,831 MW, meaning that the committed supply is less than what would be required to meet the one-event-in-10-year reliability standard.
verbatim_list: The price came in at the FERC-approved cap, $325/MW-day (UCAP) for the entire PJM footprint, a 2.5% decrease from the 2027/2028 Base Residual Auction cap of $333.44/MW-day.

These most recent auctions were the first in PJM history in which the entire RTO fell short of the reliability requirement. PJM plans to seek FERC approval to hold a special “Backstop Procurement” in September to help address the near-term shortfall in electricity supply.
The auction cleared 525 MW UCAP of new generation and generation uprates.

PJM Interconnection today announced the results of its 2028/2029 Base Residual Auction, which secured 138,318 MW of unforced capacity generation (UCAP) and demand response to meet projected electricity needs for more than 67 million people across 13 states and the District of Columbia.

title: Retirement delays of U.S. electric generating capacity may continue in 2026 (Today in Energy)
date_evidence: In-brief analysis. February 23, 2026. Retirement delays of U.S. electric generating capacity may continue in 2026
key_claim: US owners retired only 4.6 GW of the 12.3 GW planned for 2025, the least since 2008, after DOE emergency orders; 6.4 GW of coal is scheduled to retire in 2026 and renewed orders could defer that too.
frame_summary: EIA presents 2026 retirement plans as unusually contingent: the schedule exists, but federal emergency orders have already displaced 2025 retirements once and could do so again this year.
verbatim_quote: Last year, owners and operators planned to retire 12.3 GW of capacity but only retired 4.6 GW, the least since 2008, following emergency orders from the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) to extend the operations of several coal-fired plants.
verbatim_list: In 2026, 6.4 GW of coal-fired capacity is scheduled to retire, which accounts for almost 4% of the U.S. coal fleet that was in operation as of the end of 2025.
U.S. power plant owners and operators plan to retire nearly 11 gigawatts (GW) of utility-scale electric generating capacity from the U.S. power grid this year
The plans may be more subject to change than usual, with policy shifts recently delaying retirements at several coal plants.

title: Cost of coal plant emergency orders already more than $300 million
date_evidence: Cost of coal plant emergency orders already more than $300 million. June 10, 2026. Seth Feaster
key_claim: Ratepayers face at least $300 million in extra costs through mid-May from more than 20 DOE emergency orders, rising by over $30 million per month, while the covered plants burned under 1% of US power-sector coal.
frame_summary: IEEFA argues the emergency orders impose large and rising ratepayer costs with negligible reliability or coal-industry benefit, because the covered units are aged, uneconomic and mostly idle.
verbatim_quote: A year into the administration’s effort to prevent the closure of coal-fired power plants using emergency orders, an IEEFA analysis has found that ratepayers are already facing at least $300 million in extra costs through mid-May.
verbatim_list: These costs are rising by more than $30 million per month, and could soar much higher if extensive repairs are made at some units.
As of June 5, the energy department had issued 22 emergency orders for eight different power plants, requiring 12 individual generating units to stay open.
Just one plant, J.H. Campbell, accounted for 93% of the 3.03 million tons of coal used under the orders between June 2025 and March 2026.

However, as wielded by Energy Secretary Chris Wright, a former oil and gas industry executive, the 90-day orders have been used almost exclusively to prevent the retirement of aging, uneconomic coal units—some of them currently inoperable—by the electric utilities that own them.
The company said it would cost between $16.5 million and $20.5 million and take at least four weeks of downtime for maintenance to prevent “an increasing risk of catastrophic mechanical failure.”

Consumers says it has cost at least $185 million to keep it open for the 10 months through March 31—and that figure could rise as much as $90 million more by the time the current emergency order expires on Aug. 16.
The total amount of coal used by the plants under the emergency orders amounted to less than 1% of the coal used by all U.S. plants to produce power in the same period.

title: Review of NERC's 2026 Summer Reliability Assessment
key_claim: Supplementing NERC's assessment with Lawrence Berkeley National Lab queue data, Grid Strategies finds both US elevated-risk regions resource adequate even under extreme conditions, with all regions holding 5% to 93% more reserves than target.
frame_summary: Grid Strategies argues NERC's elevated-risk designations overstate the danger because likely-to-connect queue resources, non-firm imports and operational mitigations close the gap without holding retiring plants open.
verbatim_quote: This more comprehensive picture of likely-to-connect resources—plus non-firm imports from neighboring regions and operational mitigation strategies—enables all regions to have between 5% – 93% more reserves than their target reserve margin.
verbatim_list: In its 2026 SRA, NERC projected all areas to have adequate resources for normal summer conditions, but identified two regions in the U.S.—New England and Northwest—at “elevated risk” in meeting once-in-a-decade extreme load conditions.

title: Power plants under DOE emergency orders are producing way less energy than before
key_claim: Five plants under retirement-deferral orders produced 1.5 million MWh in Q1 2026, down 65% year on year; two produced nothing, and never before had DOE ordered units to run past scheduled retirement.
frame_summary: Utility Dive's data analysis argues the ordered plants are running far below historic output, several not at all, which undercuts the emergency rationale while owners incur repair costs and pursue appeals.
verbatim_quote: Combined, five of the power plants produced 1.5 million MWh in the first quarter of this year under the DOE’s orders, down 65% from the 4.3 million MWh they generated in the same period last year.
verbatim_list: Never before in the Energy Department’s nearly 50-year history has it ordered generating units to continue producing power after their scheduled retirement dates.
To do so, it has used  a string of 90-day emergency orders issued under the Federal Power Act’s section 202(c). DOE has reissued those orders for all the units before the initial orders expired.
Tri-State and Platte River on April 29 asked the U.S. Appeals Court for the District of Columbia Circuit to overturn the DOE’s first 202(c) order for Craig Unit 1.
The Department of Energy ordered six power plants to delay their retirements last year. Two of them produced zero electricity in the first quarter of 2026, and another one is now offline for repairs.
